Sixty-four localities have been sampled so far from the Mesozoic and Palaeogene. The samples were measured on JR-4 spinner magnetometers with an r.m.s. noise level of 4. 10e6 A/m. Seven andesite and thirty-three sediment collections yielded useful palaeomagnetic results (Fig. 1 and Table I), whereas the remainder were too weak for precise measurements. On calculating the locality means in Table I, some of the samples had to be disregarded either due to low intensity as in localities Nos, 2, 4, 7, 8, 29, and 33, or overprinted magnetization, which means that samples with imperfectly removed overprint were rejected and the locality mean was based on apparently single- component remanence as in localities 6, 15, 16, 22, 24, 25, 27, 28 and 30. Recently obtained palaeomagnetic data have given a fairly detailed apparent polar wander (A.P.W.) curve for the Mesozoic of the Transdanubian Central Mountains which has been compared with other A.P.W. curves from the Mediterranean area. The similarity of the A.P.W. curves enabled a unified A.P.W. curve to be constructed for the Central Mediterranean region. It has been shown that the new Mediterranean A.P.W. curve is in full agreement, even in details, with the updated A.P.W. curve for Africa. This confirms the existence during the entire Mesozoic of a single Central Mediterranean mega- tectonic unit rigidly attached to Africa. Its positions with respect to the pole can now be traced back in more detail than before. IN

The outcrops of the Mesozoic formations of the same age form southwest-northeast trending zones. In the southeast, Palaeozoic and Triassic rocks occur. The former includes a granite area with outcrops of Eocene andesite. The median zone is occupied by Jurassic and Cretaceous formations while the narrow northeast strip consists of Triassic rocks. Structurally, these formations are believed to form an autochthonous asymmetrical synclinorium that folded before the Senonian (Ftilop, 1968). A palaeomagnetic study of the Helmsdale granite (U/Pb-420 m.y., K/Ar-400 m.y.), northeast Scotland, has revealed a multicomponent remanence dominated by two characteristic axes of magnetiza- tion. The suggested oldest of these magnetizations, the direction of which is nearly horizontal and directed N-S, is thought to have been acquired in Upper Silurian-Lower Devonian times. The existence of this shallow direction of magnetization discounts a recent hypothesis of a ea. 2000 km sinistral offset along the Great Glen Fault. The second component of ma~et~tion appears to be partly carried by haematite that apparently formed through disintegration of biotite and/or plagiociase. This secondary magnetization has a direction that can be associated with a Permian-early Mesozoic age. Similar overprinted magnetizations are characteristic features also in the Devonian sedimentary sequences north of Helmsdale. The present paper reports on the magnetic properties of the Helmsdale granite (Fig. 1) and discusses tectonic implications. The Helmsdale granite was emplaced into metasedimentary rocks of the Moine series. To the northeast and southwest Devonian sandstone overlies the granite. and along the coast it is bounded by the Helmsdale fault. The rock is a pink adamellite with approximately equal proportions of quarts, K-feldspar and plagioclase. The granite is relatively unaffected by tectonic events since its emplacement in Upper Silurian-Lower Devonian time. Haematite is the dominant oxide mineral, being present in association with plagioclase, biotite and chlorite, often occurring along micro-cracs. Plagioclase is characterized by anhedral to subhedral grains, and is generally intensely altered, especially in the inner anorthite-rich areas of the crystals. The most common alteration products are fine-grained mica, aggregates of iron-hydroxides, haematite and chlorite. the Middle Devonian strata of Caithness invalidates the model, proposed by Van der Voo and Scotese (1981), involving a ca. 2000 km sinistral offset along the Great Glen Fault in the Carboniferous. However, the available data are in favour of a few hundred kilometres sinistral movement along this fracture zone. However, the possibility of there having been a much larger transcurrent shift between Europe and North America in late/post-Devonian times, accumulated along various fracture zones within the Caledonian fold belt, is discussed. On the basis of an inferred overprinted magnetization, it is tentatively concluded that the tectonic deformation of the Old Red Sandstone of Caithness has a mid-Jurassic or younger age. This survey involves both re-examination of earlier work as well as studies of new rocks. Storetvedt (1974) has suggested the existence of a ca. 15O discordance in Devonian palaeom

The earlier study of these beds (Waage and Storetvedt, 1973) encountered severe experimental problems in determining high temperature single-component magnetizations, and palaeomagnetic field directions were successfully unravelled from only very few specimens. Some of the sites, however, showed promising potential for further analysis, providing a strong impetus for the present study. The rock material for the extended demagnetization work reported here comes from the same oriented block samples that formed the basis for the previous investigation. Due to lack of storage capacity the hand samples collected were discarded at an early stage, after a total of 111 :” cylindrical specimens had been cut from them. 70 of these specimens were studied in the original investigation and the remaining 41 are included in the present analysis. The series of the Rotliegende, which reaches a thickness of about 2000 m, consists of fluviatile and limnic sediments interbedded with volcanic rocks. INTRODUCTION The geotectonic history of the Iberian peninsula as a continental block has been documented by paleomagnetic data which indicate a counterclockwise rotation of 35” relative to stable Europe. This rotation occurred between Barremian-Aptian and Maastrichtian time (VandenBerg, 1980). The relative position of the Internal Zone of the Betic Cordilleras-the alpine foldbelt of southern Spain-is, however, unknown for its entire history prior to the Miocene when it became attached to Iberia (Kampschuur and Rondeel, 1975). The Internal Zone consists of a number of nappe complexes that underwent considerable deformation prior to the deposition of Middle Miocene sediments (Rondeel and Simon, 1974). The metamorphic complexes comprise Nevado-Filabride * Present address: Koninklijke/Shell Exploratie & Produktie Laboratorium, Volmerlaan 6, 2288 CD Rijswijk, The Netherlands. 0040-1951/84/$03.00 0 1984 Elsevier Science Publishers B.V. 132 units, Alpujarride units and in addition in the eastern part, the Almagro and the Ballabona-Cucharon units. All of these complexes mainly contain sediments of Triassic and older age. The essentially non-metamorphic Malaguide Complex that tectonically overlies the Alpujarride Complex contains restricted amounts of younger

exes mainly contain sediments of Triassic and older age. The essentially non-metamorphic Malaguide Complex that tectonically overlies the Alpujarride Complex contains restricted amounts of younger rocks. The Internal Zone is in tectonic contact with the External Zone of the Betic Cordilleras (Fig. 1). The External Zone can be subdivided in a (par)autochthonous Prebetic realm in the north and an allochtonous Subbetic in the south. In the Miocene the Subbetic has been thrust, in northern direction, over parts of the Prebetic. The External Zone contains deformed Triassic, Jurassic and Cretaceous sediments which are considered to be deposited on the southern continental margin of the Iberian block (Hermes, 1978; Garcia-Hernandez et al.. 1980). INTRODUCTION The geotectonic history of the Iberian peninsula as a continental block has been documented by paleomagnetic data which indicate a counterclockwise rotation of 35” relative to stable Europe. This rotation occurred between Barremian-Aptian and Maastrichtian time (VandenBerg, 1980). The relative position of the Internal Zone of the Betic Cordilleras-the alpine foldbelt of southern Spain-is, however, unknown for its entire history prior to the Miocene when it became attached to Iberia (Kampschuur and Rondeel, 1975). The Internal Zone consists of a number of nappe complexes that underwent considerable deformation prior to the deposition of Middle Miocene sediments (Rondeel and Simon, 1974). The metamorphic complexes comprise Nevado-Filabride * Present address: Koninklijke/Shell Exploratie & Produktie Laboratorium, Volmerlaan 6, 2288 CD Rijswijk, The Netherlands. 0040-1951/84/$03.00 0 1984 Elsevier Science Publishers B.V. 132 units, Alpujarride units and in addition in the eastern part, the Almagro and the Ballabona-Cucharon units. All of these complexes mainly contain sediments of Triassic and older age. The essentially non-metamorphic Malaguide Complex that tectonically overlies the Alpujarride Complex contains restricted amounts of younger

exes mainly contain sediments of Triassic and older age. The essentially non-metamorphic Malaguide Complex that tectonically overlies the Alpujarride Complex contains restricted amounts of younger rocks. The Internal Zone is in tectonic contact with the External Zone of the Betic Cordilleras (Fig. 1). The External Zone can be subdivided in a (par)autochthonous Prebetic realm in the north and an allochtonous Subbetic in the south. In the Miocene the Subbetic has been thrust, in northern direction, over parts of the Prebetic. The External Zone contains deformed Triassic, Jurassic and Cretaceous sediments which are considered to be deposited on the southern continental margin of the Iberian block (Hermes, 1978; Garcia-Hernandez et al.. 1980). The,amphibolite suite was intruded between the Carn Chuinneag granite (ca. 560 Ma) and the late Caledonian pegmatites at ca. 450 Ma (Smith, 1979). The microdiorite-appinite suite cuts the 450 Ma pegmatites and predates the Strontian and Ross of Mull granites intruded at 420 Ma (Beckinsale and Obradovich, 1973; Smith, 1979). Thus the rocks of this study (excepting the lamprophyres) were uplifted and cooled with the regional metamorphic terrain and have a magnetic remanence record related, at least in part, to this post-tectonic late Caledonian event. Theoretical aspects of the acquisition of remanence during slow cooling have been treated by a number of workers (Ueno et al., 1975; Pullaiah et al., 1975; Dodson and McClelland Brown, 1980). The analysis of the latter workers shows that the magnetic blocking temperatures of rocks subject to the cooling rates of the Caledonides are only slightly lower than the unblocking temperatures determined in the laboratory implying that the uplift magnetisations are appreciably older than the K-Ar mineral ages. target_context.excerpt: erogenic belt and its Precambrian foreland zone between the Great Glen Fault (GGF) zone to the southeast and the Laurentian Block to the northwest, we have studied the palaeomagnetism of minor intrusive rocks within the Northern Highlands terrain. These rocks include (1) amphibolites and other metamorphic rocks predating deformation, (2) microdiorities, dolerites and related suites emplaced, and probably magnetised, between 450 and 420 Ma, and (3) Lower-Middle Devonian lamprophyres. A range of predominantly NNE negative and SSW positive components are resolved by cleaning treatment with a dispersion of declinations towards a minority WNW-ESE axis; isolated southerly negative directed hematite-held components su

uplift magnetisations were therefore acquired at greater depths than these. Dewey and Pankhurst (1970) accept the maximum rate of subsidence of 0.25 km/Ma in the South Mayo Trough as a possible maximum uplift rate in the Scottish Highlands, close to the lower end of the range of uplift rates of 0.8-0.2 km/Ma from Alpine and Andean erogenic belts. Minor intrusions, in the form of narrow parallel-sided bodies ranging from dykes to low-angle sheets, are widely distributed in the Northern Highlands (Smith, 1979) being very numerous in the southwestern sector and less important towards the north-northeast. They are subdivided into a number of suites by intersecting relationships each one representing a phase of magma

Thus the rocks of this study (excepting the lamprophyres) were uplifted and cooled with the regional metamorphic terrain and have a magnetic remanence record related, at least in part, to this post-tectonic late Caledonian event. Theoretical aspects of the acquisition of remanence during slow cooling have been treated by a number of workers (Ueno et al., 1975; Pullaiah et al., 1975; Dodson and McClelland Brown, 1980). The analysis of the latter workers shows that the magnetic blocking temperatures of rocks subject to the cooling rates of the Caledonides are only slightly lower than the unblocking temperatures determined in the laboratory implying that the uplift magnetisations are appreciably older than the K-Ar mineral ages. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: To evaluate the scale of tectonic movements within the northern sector of the 500-400 Ma Caledonian erogenic belt and its Precambrian foreland zone between the Great Glen Fault (GGF) zone to the southeast and the Laurentian Block to the northwest, we have studied the palaeomagnetism of minor intrusive rocks within the Northern Highlands terrain. These rocks include (1) amphibolites and other metamorphic rocks predating deformation, (2) microdiorities, dolerites and related suites emplaced, and probably magnetised, between 450 and 420 Ma, and (3) Lower-Middle Devonian lamprophyres. A range of predominantly NNE negative and SSW positive components are resolved by cleaning treatment with a dispersion of declinations towards a minority WNW-ESE axis; isolated southerly negative directed hematite-held components suggests limited, but no widespread, remagnetisation in Devonian-Carbonifer- ous times. Comparison is made with data from other tectonic divisions in the Caledonian erogenic belt and the bordering forelands. Palaeopoles from the Northern Highlands closely conform in part with North American Ordovician poles and in part with the post-Ordovician palaeopoles from Britain south of the GGF. To evaluate the scale of tectonic movements within the northern sector of the 500-400 Ma Caledonian erogenic belt and its Precambrian foreland zone between the Great Glen Fault (GGF) zone to the southeast and the Laurentian Block to the northwest, we have studied the palaeomagnetism of minor intrusive rocks within the Northern Highlands terrain. These rocks include (1) amphibolites and other metamorphic rocks predating deformation, (2) microdiorities, dolerites and related suites emplaced, and probably magnetised, between 450 and 420 Ma, and (3) Lower-Middle Devonian lamprophyres. A range of predominantly NNE negative and SSW positive components are resolved by cleaning treatment with a dispersion of declinations towards a minority WNW-ESE axis; isolated southerly negative directed hematite-held components suggests limited, but no widespread, remagnetisation in Devonian-Carbonifer- ous times. Comparison is made with data from other tectonic divisions in the Caledonian erogenic belt and the bordering forelands. Palaeopoles from the Northern Highlands closely con

age and genetically linked to the younger granites; they cut most of these granites and occur as pebbles in the basal conglomerates of the Middle Old Red Sandstone sediments. The,amphibolite suite was intruded between the Carn Chuinneag granite (ca. 560 Ma) and the late Caledonian pegmatites at ca. 450 Ma (Smith, 1979). The microdiorite-appinite suite cuts the 450 Ma pegmatites and predates the Strontian and Ross of Mull granites intruded at 420 Ma (Beckinsale and Obradovich, 1973; Smith, 1979). Thus the rocks of this study (excepting the lamprophyres) were uplifted and cooled with the regional metamorphic terrain and have a magnetic remanence record related, at least in part, to this post-tectonic late Caledonian event. Theoretical aspects of the acquisition of remanence during slow cooling have been treated by a number of workers (Ueno et al., 1975; Pullaiah et al., 1975; Dodson and McClelland Brown, 1980). The analysis of the latter workers shows that the magnetic blocking temperatures of rocks subject to the cooling rates of the Caledonides are only slightly lower than the unblocking temperatures determined in the laboratory implying that the uplift magnetisations are appreciably older than the K-Ar mineral ages. retical aspects of the acquisition of remanence during slow cooling have been treated by a number of workers (Ueno et al., 1975; Pullaiah et al., 1975; Dodson and McClelland Brown, 1980). The analysis of the latter workers shows that the magnetic blocking temperatures of rocks subject to the cooling rates of the Caledonides are only slightly lower than the unblocking temperatures determined in the laboratory implying that the uplift magnetisations are appreciably older than the K-Ar mineral ages. Some practical studies of uplift magnetisations in Precambrian rocks (Morgan 1976, Piper 1981) identify some of the main characteristics of remanence acquisition under conditions of slow cooling, namely the averaging of short term secular features of the magnetic field and the recording of time sequences of palaeopoles by higher to lower blocking temperature phases and earlier to later-cooled facies. Uplift rates in the Caledonides were at least an order more rapid than these Proterozoic terrains (Piper, 1981; Dewey and Pankhurst, 1970) and two features of palaeomagnetic behaviour characterise this Caledonian collection; the first is a tendancy for single units to record directions of both normal and reversed polarity generally in different phases (magnetite and hematite) but some

both normal and reversed polarity generally in different phases (magnetite and hematite) but sometimes in the same phase, and the second is a tendancy for sample directions within individual sites to be smeared in a distribu- tion which is not effectively reduced by cleaning and frequently lies along part of a great circle incorporating normal and reversed field axes. Systematic migration of sample directions back along an ancient a.p.w. trend with progressive cleaning (Morgan, 1976) has not been positively identified possibly because the cooling rate was too fast for blocking temperature spectra to record a significant path length. PALAEOMAGNETIC RESULTS Field and laboratory methods Cores drilled in the field were oriented by sights on the Sun and/or magnetic bearings in conjunction with topographic sights. A site normally comprises six or seven independently-oriented cores from one geological unit but up to 30 cores were drilled at some sites in Moinian metasediments. To evaluate the scale of tectonic movements within the northern sector of the 500-400 Ma Caledonian erogenic belt and its Precambrian foreland zone between the Great Glen Fault (GGF) zone to the southeast and the Laurentian Block to the northwest, we have studied the palaeomagnetism of minor intrusive rocks within the Northern Highlands terrain. These rocks include (1) amphibolites and other metamorphic rocks predating deformation, (2) microdiorities, dolerites and related suites emplaced, and probably magnetised, between 450 and 420 Ma, and (3) Lower-Middle Devonian lamprophyres. A range of predominantly NNE negative and SSW positive components are resolved by cleaning treatment with a dispersion of declinations towards a minority WNW-ESE axis; isolated southerly negative directed hematite-held components suggests limited, but no widespread, remagnetisation in Devonian-Carbonifer- ous times. Comparison is made with data from other tectonic divisions in the Caledonian erogenic belt and the bordering forelands. Palaeopoles from the Northern Highlands closely con

age and genetically linked to the younger granites; they cut most of these granites and occur as pebbles in the basal conglomerates of the Middle Old Red Sandstone sediments. The,amphibolite suite was intruded between the Carn Chuinneag granite (ca. 560 Ma) and the late Caledonian pegmatites at ca. 450 Ma (Smith, 1979). The microdiorite-appinite suite cuts the 450 Ma pegmatites and predates the Strontian and Ross of Mull granites intruded at 420 Ma (Beckinsale and Obradovich, 1973; Smith, 1979). Thus the rocks of this study (excepting the lamprophyres) were uplifted and cooled with the regional metamorphic terrain and have a magnetic remanence record related, at least in part, to this post-tectonic late Caledonian event. Theoretical aspects of the acquisition of remanence during slow cooling have been treated by a number of workers (Ueno et al., 1975; Pullaiah et al., 1975; Dodson and McClelland Brown, 1980). The analysis of the latter workers shows that the magnetic blocking temperatures of rocks subject to the cooling rates of the Caledonides are only slightly lower than the unblocking temperatures determined in the laboratory implying that the uplift magnetisations are appreciably older than the K-Ar mineral ages. Paleomagnetic measurements have been conducted on the M&Pliocene series along the external sedimentary Hellenic arc, in order td detect the presence or absence of rotational deformations in different sections of the arc. In the central-eastern part of the arc (Crete and Rhodes) paleomagnetic directions are very closely aligned along the North-South direction, showing that this portion of the arc has not undergone significant rotation since at least 7 m.y. (for Crete) and 4 m.y. (for Rhodes). In the western and northwestern parts, results from South Peloponnesos, Zakinthos, Kephallinia and Corfu indicate that this section of the arc has undergone a clockwise rotation. Detailed analysis of the data from the three Ionian islands shows that their rotation began about 5 m.y. B.P. and has proceeded since then at roughly 5

s direction in a zone of sinistral strike-slip faulting. These different motions have given rise to different underwater topographies in the two branches of the trench, which have been studied by seabeam and submarine surveys (Le Pichon et al., 1979a and b). The external arc along the trenches is subjected to compressional or strike-slip earthquakes whose slip vectors are directed roughly along the N48 direction in the west and along N22 in the east (Le Pichon et al., 1979a and b). The compressional zone of the external arc affects emerged lands only at the northwestern termination, in the Ionian Islands, where these compressional deformations (probably responsible for the present margin) began during the early Pliocene and were still active during the Pleistocene (Mercier et al., 1976). The great extent of these compressive struc- tures makes this region quite different from the rest of Aegea: indeed, the internal Aegean regions have been essentially submitted to a large scale extensional regime since the upper Miocene, and this regime has only occasionally been interrupted by compressive events, often quite moderate, in the upper Miocene-lower Pliocene and lower Pleistocene periods. Focal mechanism solutions show that the present regime is still extensional in all the

htly away from the external trenches, such as South Pelopon- nesos, Crete and Rhodes (McKenzie, 1972, 1978; Ritsema, 1973, 1974). In each of these regions, present-day stress directions, calculated from focal mechanisms or from in-situ measurements, are very close to the stress directions since the middle Pleistocene, as determined from the analysis of neotectonic faults and striations (Paquin et al., 1982, this volume). Thus, neotectonic analysis has allowed us to reconstruct the successive stress patterns in the Aegean arc since the upper Miocene. Using stress pattern analysis, different authors have considered the problem of the deformation of Aegea, and have suggested models for the geodynamical evolu- tion of the Aegean arc. Even if all the models come to the conclusion that the curvature of the arc has been acquired at least partially because of its tectonic evolution, the geodynamical mechanisms involved are substantially different accord- ing to the different authors. For instance Brunn (1976), Fig. 1, has suggested a model of continuous deforma- tion in which the curvature of the arc is related to the main Tertiary Alpine overthrustings, and was thus essentially completed before the neotectonic period. Since the 1979 survey, a portable spinner magnetometer (Chiron et al., 1981) has been used systematically to select sites with a minimum magnetization level, which has been fixed at 10F6 emu/cm, among those which are geologically significant. An electrical machine mounted on a frame and powered by a portable generator was used to drill the samples. The corer is a 25mm bronze barrel, 150 mm long, with a sintered diamond cutting edge. Water was sometimes used as a coolant but, as a routine, compressed air was used to cool the corer and to remove the dust, and this technique proved to be fast and lightweight. Orientation of cores was done with a special device. Even though the sediments have a very weak magnetism, a sun compass was used whenever possible, because it allows a more precise comparison between the directions of very distant sites (no corrections for regional magnetic anomalies are needed). The accuracy on orienta- tion is about 2”. A total of more than 2300 cores has been collected from 135 sites in the Aegean arc. Paleomagnetic measurements have been conducted on the M&Pliocene series along the external sedimentary Hellenic arc, in order td detect the presence or absence of rotational deformations in different sections of the arc. In the central-eastern part of the arc (Crete and Rhodes) paleomagnetic directions are very closely aligned along the North-South direction, showing that this portion of the arc has not undergone significant rotation since at least 7 m.y. (for Crete) and 4 m.y. (for Rhodes). In the western and northwestern parts, results from South Peloponnesos, Zakinthos, Kephallinia and Corfu indicate that this section of the arc has undergone a clockwise rotation. Detailed analysis of the data from the three Ionian islands shows that their rotation began about 5 m.y. B.P. and has proceeded since then at roughly 5

s direction in a zone of sinistral strike-slip faulting. These different motions have given rise to different underwater topographies in the two branches of the trench, which have been studied by seabeam and submarine surveys (Le Pichon et al., 1979a and b). The external arc along the trenches is subjected to compressional or strike-slip earthquakes whose slip vectors are directed roughly along the N48 direction in the west and along N22 in the east (Le Pichon et al., 1979a and b). The compressional zone of the external arc affects emerged lands only at the northwestern termination, in the Ionian Islands, where these compressional deformations (probably responsible for the present margin) began during the early Pliocene and were still active during the Pleistocene (Mercier et al., 1976). The great extent of these compressive struc- tures makes this region quite different from the rest of Aegea: indeed, the internal Aegean regions have been essentially submitted to a large scale extensional regime since the upper Miocene, and this regime has only occasionally been interrupted by compressive events, often quite moderate, in the upper Miocene-lower Pliocene and lower Pleistocene periods. Focal mechanism solutions show that the present regime is still extensional in all the

htly away from the external trenches, such as South Pelopon- nesos, Crete and Rhodes (McKenzie, 1972, 1978; Ritsema, 1973, 1974). In each of these regions, present-day stress directions, calculated from focal mechanisms or from in-situ measurements, are very close to the stress directions since the middle Pleistocene, as determined from the analysis of neotectonic faults and striations (Paquin et al., 1982, this volume). Thus, neotectonic analysis has allowed us to reconstruct the successive stress patterns in the Aegean arc since the upper Miocene. Using stress pattern analysis, different authors have considered the problem of the deformation of Aegea, and have suggested models for the geodynamical evolu- tion of the Aegean arc. Even if all the models come to the conclusion that the curvature of the arc has been acquired at least partially because of its tectonic evolution, the geodynamical mechanisms involved are substantially different accord- ing to the different authors. For instance Brunn (1976), Fig. 1, has suggested a model of continuous deforma- tion in which the curvature of the arc is related to the main Tertiary Alpine overthrustings, and was thus essentially completed before the neotectonic period. Since the 1979 survey, a portable spinner magnetometer (Chiron et al., 1981) has been used systematically to select sites with a minimum magnetization level, which has been fixed at 10F6 emu/cm, among those which are geologically significant. An electrical machine mounted on a frame and powered by a portable generator was used to drill the samples. The corer is a 25mm bronze barrel, 150 mm long, with a sintered diamond cutting edge. Water was sometimes used as a coolant but, as a routine, compressed air was used to cool the corer and to remove the dust, and this technique proved to be fast and lightweight. Orientation of cores was done with a special device. Even though the sediments have a very weak magnetism, a sun compass was used whenever possible, because it allows a more precise comparison between the directions of very distant sites (no corrections for regional magnetic anomalies are needed). The blue-grey colour itself is probably not the original colour of the sediments, but a result of chemical reduction phenomena due to their organic contents. Pyritized concretions very frequently observed in Foraminifera shells, for instance, are good evidence of iron migration in the sediment. Thus, in the model presented at this conference, Crete is “decoupled” from Peloponnesos and does not show any appreciable rotation. All these models are based on seismic and tectonic data. An important parameter which cannot be attained by these methods is the rotational deformation and its variations along the arc. Recent progress in both the technology and understanding of the pal~magnetism of sedimentary rocks now allows the use of their weak remanent magnetization for geological purposes. ies. The extent of these internal defo~ations has led Mercier (1977) and Mercier et al. (1976, 1979) to the notion of the continuum of deformation. In their opinion, the Aegean domain constitutes the plastically deformed edge of the Euro-Asiatic plate. The prolongation of the northern Anatolian strike-slip faults into the northwestern Aegean Sea and the discovery of faults with a sinistral strike-slip component in Macedonia have led Mercier et al. (1979) to consider that the defo~ation of this region of northern Aegea may be described by a scheme of slip lines, as suggested by Tapponnier. This evolutionary scheme implies rotational deformations of the Aegean lithosphere, clockwise in the northwest and anticlockwise in the southeast of the arc, Le Pichon and Angelier (1979) consider the neotectonic movement since 13 m.y. to be a first appro~mation of the clockwise rotation of a rigid plate by approx. 30” about an eulerian pole, located near 4WN, 18’E in the southern Adriatic Sea. f a rigid plate by approx. 30” about an eulerian pole, located near 4WN, 18’E in the southern Adriatic Sea. An important back arc distension, indicated by intensive normal faulting in the Aegean Sea, is superimposed upon this rigid rotation and modifies its value locally all along the external arc: there is thus maximum rotation in the northwest (Ionian Islands except Corfu) decreasing towards the southeast to attain zero near eastern Crete. According to them, western Crete appears to undergo a clockwise rotation, causing a torsion of the island. More recently (Lybbris et al., 1980, 1981) the discovery of longitudinal variations of deformation in the Kithiran strait as shown by seabeam bathymetric studies and by the existence of en echelon faults, has led these authors to modify their original model. Thus, in the model presented at this conference, Crete is “decoupled” from Peloponnesos and does not show any appreciable rotation. All these models are based on seismic and tectonic data. An important parameter which cannot be attained by these methods is the rotational deformation and its variations along the arc. Paleomagnetic measurements have been conducted on the M&Pliocene series along the external sedimentary Hellenic arc, in order td detect the presence or absence of rotational deformations in different sections of the arc. In the central-eastern part of the arc (Crete and Rhodes) paleomagnetic directions are very closely aligned along the North-South direction, showing that this portion of the arc has not undergone significant rotation since at least 7 m.y. (for Crete) and 4 m.y. (for Rhodes). An important back arc distension, indicated by intensive normal faulting in the Aegean Sea, is superimposed upon this rigid rotation and modifies its value locally all along the external arc: there is thus maximum rotation in the northwest (Ionian Islands except Corfu) decreasing towards the southeast to attain zero near eastern Crete. According to them, western Crete appears to undergo a clockwise rotation, causing a torsion of the island. Paleomagnetic investigations of Mesozoic and Paleozoic rocks from S&bard. In: E.S. Husebye, G.L. Johnson and Y. Kristoffersen (Editors), Geophysics of the Polar Regions. Tectonophysics, 114: 163-180. A paleomagnetic study of Late Mesozoic dolerite dykes and sills and Paleozoic sediments from Spitsbergen, the main island of the Svalbard Archipelago, gives the position of the pole in the Late Mesozoic and Paleozoic as distinct from the corresponding poles of Europe and North America. The Paleozoic pole is to the south of corresponding poles for Europe and North America. The data suggest that Svalbard has moved independently of Europe and North America at least in the Late Mesozoic, and thus might behave as a microplate or block. A paleomagnetic study of Late Mesozoic dolerite dykes and sills and Paleozoic sediments from Spitsbergen, the main island of the Svalbard Archipelago, gives the position of the pole in the Late Mesozoic and Paleozoic as distinct from the corresponding poles of Europe and North America. The Paleozoic pole is to the south of corresponding poles for Europe and North America. The data suggest that Svalbard has moved independently of Europe and North America at least in the Late Mesozoic, and thus might behave as a microplate or block. An important fracturing appears to have controlled the distribu- tion of the effects of this metamorphism. The temperature conditions remained relatively low, certainly below 400°C. GEOLOGICAL SETTING OF THE NORTHERN VOSGES The Vosges Massif is divided structuratly into two parts by an important fault trending E-W, called the “Lalaye-Lubine dislocation”. The domain, situated to the north, belongs to the Saxothuringian zone (Kossmat, 1927) whereas the southern one is part of the Moldanubian zone. This zone of dislocation successively acted as a south-dipping thrust fault and then as a dextral strike-slip fault with an offset of about 100 km (Edel, 1982). PALEOMAGNETIC SAMPLING AND LABORATORY TECHNIQUES Oriented samples were drilled in situ or collected as handsamples. Whenever possible, they were oriented both with a solar and a magnetic compass. The handsamples were cored in the laboratory and the cores subsequently cut into standard specimens 2.5 cm long. Remanent magnetization measurements were performed on a computerized Digico magnetometer, with noise level reduced to 3 . lo-’ Am-‘. Susceptibilities were determined with a Digico susceptibility bridge. The alternating field and thermal demagnetizations were done with laboratory-made apparatus. NATURAL REMANENT MAGNETIZATIONS AND SUSCEPTIBILITIES High magnetic anomalies of up to 300 nT at 1200 m above sea level overlie the northern Vosges. They belong to a band of anomalies which extends from the Paris Basin to the Thuringerwald (Edel. 1982). Their origin is attributed to the magnetic properties of granodiorites, diorites and rocks of contact metamorphism (Lauer and Taktak, 1971; Edel and Lauer, 1974; Lauer, 1975; Gancarski, 1977). The results presented here were obtained from plutonic and volcano-sedimentary units from the northern Vosges. The objectives of the study were first to improve our knowledge of the magnetic properties of the plutons, second to assess the impact. in terms of rock magnetism, of their intrusion on the surrounding host rocks and third to check whether the basement on both sides of the Lalaye-Lubine fault, which delimits the northern Vosges from the middle and southern, underwent simifar motions in Carboniferous times. K-Ar dating of plutonics on extracted minerals was carried out in order to assign ages to the successive magnetizations. GEOLOGICAL SETTING OF THE NORTHERN VOSGES The Vosges Massif is divided structuratly into two parts by an important fault trending E-W, called the “Lalaye-Lubine dislocation”. The domain, situated to the north, belongs to the Saxothuringian zone (Kossmat, 1927) whereas the southern one is part of the Moldanubian zone. This zone of dislocation successively acted as a south-dipping thrust fault and then as a dextral strike-slip fault with an offset of about 100 km (Edel, 1982). Since the Permian Nideck-Donon ignimbrites indicate a similar direction (Roche et al., 1962) the emplacement of magnetizations can be considered to be late. The A-direction belongs to the Kiaman reversed interval with a corresponding VGP which is consistent with European poles, i.e. the latest Carboniferous and Permian poles (Fig. 5). It has to be noted that this VGP is unique in the northern Vosges. The B,-direction is exhibited as a primary magnetization in the Kagenfels rhyolite and as overprinting in the neighbouring series, granodiorites and schists. A K-ear determination on biotite from the Kagenfels granite indicates an age of 284 Ma which corresponds to the Carboniferous-Permian boundary. Closely similar direc- tions exist in the northern and northeastern Massif Central (Edel et al.. 1981 b: Edel, 1984) where they have been observed in Carboniferous volcanics, plutons and amphibolites (Fig. 6). In the latter formation, the mean direction: D = 247”. I = 3.5” (VGP: 14”N. 1lO”E) represents an overprinting related to leucogranite intrusion dated at 312 Ma (Edel, 1984). Further west

is observed with mean direction D = 238”, I= - 8” (VGP: 24”N, 112”E) of which the declination can be compared with the reversed B,. This latter overprint occurred after the early Westphalian. Wandering of the paleomagnetic directions from B to A cannot be simply explained by tilting of the Champ du Feu massif to the southeast, since the dip would exceed 70”. Thus we are compelled to assume a StephanianAutunian clockwise rotation of the northern Vosges relative to the “stable Europe”. If the B,-direction is considered, the angle of rotation is about 30”. It reaches 70” with the B,-direction. Because of the uncertainty of magnetization polarity a counterclock- wise rotation would also be a possible but very unlikely solution. We have interpre- ted the late Variscan clockwise rotations in the Armorican Massif and the Massif Central as a consequence of the latest tightening phases of the Iberian-Armorican arc. These magnetizations probably took place after the latest metamorphic event, during a cooling phase between 335 Ma and 325 Ma (Kreuzer, 1975). The objectives of the study were first to improve our knowledge of the magnetic properties of the plutons, second to assess the impact. in terms of rock magnetism, of their intrusion on the surrounding host rocks and third to check whether the basement on both sides of the Lalaye-Lubine fault, which delimits the northern Vosges from the middle and southern, underwent simifar motions in Carboniferous times. The Carboniferous rocks of the Plaster Rock area unconformably overlie Siluro- Devonian rocks of the Chaleur Bay Synclinorium (Ruitenberg et al., 1977) which forms the eastern margin of the Matapedia Basin. This combined with the previously described “hard” (Fig. 4) magnetization, which in other studies was found to be due to the existence of fine magnetite needles in either pyroxenes (Evans et al., 1968) or in plagioclase grains (Hargraves and Young, 1969) led to a more detailed examination of the pyroxene and plagioclase grains under maximum magnification with reflected and transmitted light microscopy. Palaeomagnetic data were acquired from eighteen sampling sites situated in the main zone of the eastern Bushveld Complex, Transvaal, South Africa. Three Upper Triassic-Lower Jurassic formations in southwestern United States and northwestern Mexico have been investigated paleomagnetically as a means of testing for displacement along the proposed Mojave-Sonora megashear. Liming Formation of west-central Nevada and Sil Nakya Forma- tion of southern Arizona lie north of the megashear whereas, in northwestern Sonora, Antimonio Formation lies south of the megashear. Previously published results from the Nazas Formation of presumed Lower Jurassic age from north-central Mexico were incorporated into the interpretations. These four units compose two sets of correlative formations

(1979) smoothed apparent polar wander path for cratonic North America in the intervals 190 and 200 Ma. The displacement needed to bring all of these poles into coincidence is a pure rotation of about 8” counterclockwise about the sampling area. Two probable Cretaceous poles were obtained from the Sand Wells Formation of southern Arizona and from unnamed volcanics in northwest Sonora. These poles are essentially identical and suggest that displacement along the megashear had ceased by the Cretaceous. Data from the Early Jurassic Mulberry Wash and Pitoikam formations in southern Arizona appear to have been remagnetized in a later Cretaceous event and were not used in this study. Three Upper Triassic-Lower Jurassic formations in southwestern United States and northwestern Mexico have been investigated paleomagnetically as a means of testing for displacement along the proposed Mojave-Sonora megashear. Liming Formation of west-central Nevada and Sil Nakya Forma- tion of southern Arizona lie north of the megashear whereas, in northwestern Sonora, Antimonio Formation lies south of the megashear. Previously published results from the Nazas Formation of presumed Lower Jurassic age from north-central Mexico were incorporated into the interpretations. These four units compose two sets of correlative formations on opposite sides of the proposed megashear. Restoration of 800 km of left-lateral displacement along the megashear about the pole of rotation determined by Anderson and Schmidt (1983), improves the grouping of the two sets of paleomagnetic poles noticeably, with the improvement having statistical significance at the 95% confidence level. We feel that the data support, but do not prove, the postulated displacement along the megashear. All four poles are displaced from Irving’s (1979) smoothed apparent polar wander path for cratonic North America in the intervals 190 and 200 Ma. The displacement needed to bring all of these poles into

All cores were heated at 150°C to remove any signal residing in hydrous iron oxides, and based on the behaviour of pilot specimens (e.g. Fig. 2) higher cleaning temperatures were subsequently selected, for each locality. North-south and northwest trending suites of diabase dikes which crosscut one another have been identified in the North Carolina Piedmont from the interpretation of aeromagnetic data and field relationships (e.g., Popenoe and Zietz, 1977; Burt et al., 1978). A paleomagnetic study was conducted on the two crosscutting dike suites of the North Carolina Piedmont in order to establish whether the time differential in the emplacement of the dike suites was significant or not and to confirm relative ages. Prefolding and most probably primary remanence were isolated in Middle Cretaceous terrigenous rocks and Upper Cretaceous-Paleocene limestones and marls after stepwise thermal cleaning; only recent postfolding magnetization was found in Eocene-Oligocene clays. The Middle Cretaceous mean pole (7S” N, 153OE) agrees well with that from extra-Alpine Eurasia. A strong negative correlation between paleomagnetic inclinations and clay content in the Upper Cretaceous-Paleocene sedimentary rocks is interpreted as arising from diagenetic compaction. The limestones least affected by this process also yielded a paleopole (78O N, 179 o E) closely matching the Eurasian data. The bends of fold axes in the Kopet-Dagh are primary; tectonic rotations are discovered only within the local wrench zone in the southwestern part of the region. The close agreement of paleopoles from the Kopet-Dagh and extra-Alpine Eurasia suggests that these land masses have been welded together since the Middle Cretaceous. It was assumed that data observed might be explained by diagenetic compaction of sediments. Such a hypothesis has already been proposed (e.g., Laj et al., 1982), although without numerical evaluation. If correct, this hypothesis leads to some important conclusions: (1) As compaction of sediments takes place mainly at early stages of diagenesis, such a corre- lation implies that magnetization must be either contemporaneous with sedimentation in case of DRM or quasicontemporaneous with it in case of post-depositional DRM and early diagenetic CRM. Thus, the strong correlation between in- clination and clay content confirms the primary origin of stable magnetization in the Upper Creta- ceous-Paleocene rocks and, in general, such an approach may be used for component dating. (2) Only the largest values of inclination should be used for paleolatitude estimation. In this paper, these are the data from limestones at sites 6, 9, 10 and 11. The overall mean for all types of rocks studied will lead to errors. The steepest inclina- tions also may be shallow, but such a selection will result in minimal errors. (3) Paleomagnetism can be used, in principle, as a tool for investigation of compaction processes in sediments. This idea was challenged some years ago by the paleomagnetic data ob- tained by Vandenberg (1979) in a small Mesozoic basin located in the Asturias. Surprisingly, the Permo-Triassic redbeds yielded directions ap- parently very similar to Permo-Triassic data from stable Europe. He attempted to explain this unex- pected result by postulating the existence of a micro-plate, called “Le Danois block”, which would have behaved independently during the major movement of the Iberian plate coeval with the opening of the Bay of Biscay. The reasons supporting the assigned Permo-Triassic age to the magnetic components were: (1) Since the NRM behaved as a single compo- 0040-1951/87/$03.50 0 1987 Elsevier Science Publishers B.V. 180 nent, there was no evidence for any remagnetiza- tion. (2) Both polarities, although not exactly anti- parallel, were found. (3) The dip correction of the monoclinal struc- ture resulted in shallow inclinations consistent with the assumed Permo-Triassic age of magnetization. As there was little geological evidence support- ing Vandenberg’s hypothesis, his results called for further investigation. Our aim was mainly (1) to verify or refute Vandenberg’s paleomagnetic inter- pretation using more data, and (2) to delimit the “le Danois block” more closely. Surprisingly, the Permo-Triassic redbeds yielded directions ap- parently very similar to Permo-Triassic data from stable Europe. Surprisingly, the Permo-Triassic redbeds yielded directions ap- parently very similar to Permo-Triassic data from stable Europe. He attempted to explain this unex- pected result by postulating the existence of a micro-plate, called “Le Danois block”, which would have behaved independently during the major movement of the Iberian plate coeval with the opening of the Bay of Biscay. The reasons supporting the assigned Permo-Triassic age to the magnetic components were: (1) Since the NRM behaved as a single compo- 0040-1951/87/$03.50 0 1987 Elsevier Science Publishers B.V. 180 nent, there was no evidence for any remagnetiza- tion. This idea was challenged some years ago by the paleomagnetic data ob- tained by Vandenberg (1979) in a small Mesozoic basin located in the Asturias. Surprisingly, the Permo-Triassic redbeds yielded directions ap- parently very similar to Permo-Triassic data from stable Europe. He attempted to explain this unex- pected result by postulating the existence of a micro-plate, called “Le Danois block”, which would have behaved independently during the major movement of the Iberian plate coeval with the opening of the Bay of Biscay. The reasons supporting the assigned Permo-Triassic age to the magnetic components were: (1) Since the NRM behaved as a single compo- 0040-1951/87/$03.50 0 1987 Elsevier Science Publishers B.V. 180 nent, there was no evidence for any remagnetiza- tion. (2) Both polarities, although not exactly anti- parallel, were found. (3) The dip correction of the monoclinal struc- ture resulted in shallow inclinations consistent with the assumed Permo-Triassic age of magnetization. As there was little geological evidence support- ing Vandenberg’s hypothesis, his results called for further investigation. Our aim was mainly (1) to verify or refute Vandenberg’s paleomagnetic inter- pretation using more data, and (2) to delimit the “le Danois block” more closely. A set of thin dikes from central New Mexico, dated at 469& 7 Ma (Rb-Sr; Loring and Armstrong, 1980), have yielded a virtual geomagnetic pole which lies on the Late Paleozoic segment of the North American apparent polar wander path. The remanence of the dikes appears to be a product of Late Paleozoic hydrothermal alteration. Paradoxically, however, the magnetization of the host rocks is most simply explained in terms of a positive contact test. Samples collected between 0.2 and 0.5 dike-widths from the contact contain a component of remanence parallel to the magnetization in the dikes, with unblocking temperatures which decrease with distance from the dikes. Host rocks from a distance of more than 1 dike-width show no evidence of the characteristic dike magnetization. the Pedemal Hills, New Mexico: positive contact test in remagnetized rocks? Tectonophysics, 147: 313-323. A set of thin dikes from central New Mexico, dated at 469& 7 Ma (Rb-Sr; Loring and Armstrong, 1980), have yielded a virtual geomagnetic pole which lies on the Late Paleozoic segment of the North American apparent polar wander path. The remanence of the dikes appears to be a product of Late Paleozoic hydrothermal alteration. Paradoxically, however, the magnetization of the host rocks is most simply explained in terms of a positive contact test. Samples collected between 0.2 and 0.5 dike-widths from the contact contain a component of remanence parallel to the magnetization in the dikes, with unblocking temperatures which decrease with distance from the dikes. Host rocks from a distance of more than 1 dike-width show no evidence of the characteristic dike magnetization. There are two possible resolutions of this paradox: (1) the magnetization of the host rocks is secondary, despite the apparent positive contact test, and is a product of hydrothe~al fluid migration through the dikes or along the contact zones; or (2) the magnetization of the dikes is primary, but not representative of the Ordovician paleofield for North America. Methods Following measurement of the natural rema- nent ma~etization (NRM) of the dikes and host rocks, all samples were subjected to stepwise de- magnetization by alternating-field (AF) or thermal methods. Collinear and coplanar segments of the demagnetization trajectories were isolated by visu- al inspection of orthogonal vector projections (Zijderveld, 1967) and stereographic projections. Directions were determined by principal compo- nent analysis (Kirschvink, 1980) and means were computed using the method of Bailey and Halls (1984). Several rock magnetic experiments were per- formed in order to characterize the remanence carriers. Isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM) was imparted in a stepwise manner to a number of samples of the dike and host rocks, using an electromagnet, up to a peak field of 1.4 T. Thermomagnetic analysis of magnetic separates from several dike and host samples was performed with a horizontal Curie balance. Modified Lowrie-Fuller tests (Johnson et al., 1975) were performed in order to elucidate the domain state of magnetites in the host rock. From a stratigraphic point of view, this region is characterized by a thick Mesozoic carbonate platform, consisting of over 6000 meters of reef, back reef and dolomitic limestones, which conformably overlie an only gently deformed Paleozoic basement. A series of well stratified (150 m thick) limestones with rich microfauna, known as 'Calcari di Castro' were deposited during the Eocene and Oligocene. Although this formation is mostly of a rather coarse material, very fine grained levels can be found interbedded with the coral-algal strata. During the Miocene large amounts of calcarenites, limestones and yellow sands, the 'Pietra Leccese' formation, was also deposited over most of the region. Finally during the Pliocene and the Early Pleistocene coarse grained calcarenites and organogenic sands, known as 'Calcareniti del Salento' were deposited during marine transgressive events. From a tectonic point of view, the main feature of the Salento is the Cretaceous carbonatic-dolomitic ridge which coincides, to a lust approximation, with old Mesozoic reef zones. A shallow, southerly magnetization found at a third locality, with unblocking temperatures that range to about 500øC, has directions corresponding to a Permian (Kiaman and Alleghenian) remagnetization. section_candidates.excerpt: Appalachian carbonates affected by the Ordovician Taconic Orogeny. Geology and Sampling The structure of the study area in west-central Vermont is a product of the Taconic Orogeny during the Ordovician and is summarized by Stanley and Ratcliffe [1985]. Horizontal compression related to eastward subduction and a collision with an island arc folded the carbonate platform into the Middlebury Synclinorium. Deep-sea sediments from the continental slope and rise were incorporated into the accretionary prism and eventually were obducted onto the folded carbonate platform producing the allochthonous Taconic thrust slices. Two groups of samples were collected from the Orwell Limestone in the folded carbonate sediments of the Copyright 1988 by the American Geophysical Union. The Orwell Limestone is a fine- grained limestone dated as Mohawkian (late medial Ordovician) by ostracods, gastropods, and brachiopods [Fisher, 1977]. Orwell-2 samples (21 oriented drill cores from 3 sites) were taken from a quarry in Orwell. Each sampling group represents 5 to 10 m of section in gently dipping (less than 20 ø ) beds. This section of the Hatch Hill Formation consists of black to grey argillite beds with interbeds of dolostone, sandstone, chert breccia, and limestone. Baldwin [ 1983] has suggested a late Cambrian age for these rocks using lithostratigraphic correlations with the autochthonous shelf sequence. Hatch Hill samples (56 oriented drill-cores from 8 sites) were taken in steeply dipping to overturned beds exposed along the Poultney River. Geology and Sampling The structure of the study area in west-central Vermont is a product of the Taconic Orogeny during the Ordovician and is summarized by Stanley and Ratcliffe [1985]. Horizontal compression related to eastward subduction and a collision with an island arc folded the carbonate platform into the Middlebury Synclinorium. Deep-sea sediments from the continental slope and rise were incorporated into the accretionary prism and eventually were obducted onto the folded carbonate platform producing the allochthonous Taconic thrust slices. Geology and Sampling The structure of the study area in west-central Vermont is a product of the Taconic Orogeny during the Ordovician and is summarized by Stanley and Ratcliffe [1985]. Horizontal compression related to eastward subduction and a collision with an island arc folded the carbonate platform into the Middlebury Synclinorium. Deep-sea sediments from the continental slope and rise were incorporated into the accretionary prism and eventually were obducted onto the folded carbonate platform producing the allochthonous Taconic thrust slices. Paleomagnetism of Permo-Triassic red beds in the western Pyrenees: evidence for strong clockwise rotations of the Paleozoic units. Tectonophysics, 156: 75-88. The paleomagnetic study of Permo-Triassic red bed outcrops located in several basement units and slices of the western Pyrenees is presented. Despite strong overprintings attributed to remagnetization processes connected with the early Tertiary compressional phase, we were able to identify the original magnetization in all sites. The directions yielded reveal the occurrence, in the whole area, of clockwise rotations, varying, with respect to the European reference direction, from nearly O” to 102O. The secondary directions are interpreted as more or less contemporary with the inferred rotations. The paleomagnetic data are discussed in the light of two kinematic models for the Iberian plate. The examination of the models involving a left-lateral displacement of Iberia during the mid-Cretaceous is most conclusive and leads us to suggest that, at that time, the boundary between Europe and Iberia was located south of the Cinco-Villas and Aldudes massifs. Paleomagnetism of Permo-Triassic red beds in the western Pyrenees: evidence for strong clockwise rotations of the Paleozoic units. Tectonophysics, 156: 75-88. The paleomagnetic study of Permo-Triassic red bed outcrops located in several basement units and slices of the western Pyrenees is presented. Despite strong overprintings attributed to remagnetization processes connected with the early Tertiary compressional phase, we were able to identify the original magnetization in all sites. The directions yielded reveal the occurrence, in the whole area, of clockwise rotations, varying, with respect to the European reference direction, from nearly O” to 102O. The secondary directions are interpreted as more or less contemporary with the inferred rotations. The paleomagnetic data are discussed in the light of two kinematic models for the Iberian plate. The examination of the models involving a left-lateral displacement of Iberia during the mid-Cretaceous is most conclusive and leads us to suggest that, at that time, the boundary between Europe and Iberia was located south of the Cinco-Villas and Aldudes massifs. INTRODUCTION McWilliams and Kroner (1981) showed that the 1,2 to 0,5 Ga old palaeomagnetic poles for the Congo and Kalahari shields (a total of 41 poles) could be incorporated into a single apparent polar wander (APW) path. From this observation, they derived an ensialic model for the origin of the Damara Orogen that did not require large-scale opening and closing of ocean basins, characteristic of a Wilson-cycle process. As they clearly indicated, however, most of the palaeomagnetic poles from the Kalahari Shield lie on the 1,2 to 1 Ga portion of their APW path; whereas, most of the palaeomagnetic poles from the Congo Shield lie on the 0,9 to 0,6 Ga por

y a very few poles actually overlap from the two shields. Two of these poles were derived from a previously published palaeomagnetic study of the Gannakouriep dyke swarm (Piper, 1975a), which were referred to as the Klein Karas and the pre­ N ama dykes. The ages of these poles were purportedly-850 and -650 Ma respectively, which coincide with the peak of the tectonic evolution of the Damara Orogen. The apparent agreement of these poles with poles from the Congo Shield is obviously of paramount importance to plate tectonic models for the origin of the Damara Oro gen. For this reason, the authors undertook a detailed palaeomagnetic, petrographic, and 40Ar/39Ar study of two dykes belonging to the Gannakouriep dyke swarm with the goal of either verifying and improving upon the previously published results or refuting them. II. GEOLOGICAL SETTING The Gannakouriep dyke swarm, located in the south­ western portion of the Kalahari Shield, was defined by Reid (1979) to include north to north-east-trending mafic dykes which predate the -0,5 Ga Kuboos-Bremen granites, but which intrude the -0,9 Ga Richtersveld Suite and the basal strata of the Gariep trough (Fig. 1). INTRODUCTION McWilliams and Kroner (1981) showed that the 1,2 to 0,5 Ga old palaeomagnetic poles for the Congo and Kalahari shields (a total of 41 poles) could be incorporated into a single apparent polar wander (APW) path. From this observation, they derived an ensialic model for the origin of the Damara Orogen that did not require large-scale opening and closing of ocean basins, characteristic of a Wilson-cycle process. As they clearly indicated, however, most of the palaeomagnetic poles from the Kalahari Shield lie on the 1,2 to 1 Ga portion of their APW path; whereas, most of the palaeomagnetic poles from the Congo Shield lie on the 0,9 to 0,6 Ga portion. In fact, only a very few poles actually overlap from the two shields. Two of these poles were derived from a previously published palaeomagnetic study of the Gannakouriep dyke swarm

Abstract Two well-defined virtual geomagnetic poles (VGPs) for East Antarctica were obtained from the Middle Jurassic Ferrar Dolerite, sampled from a thick sill on Mt Schopf in the Ohio Range, and from a horizontal sheet intruding Paleozoic granitic rocks at Mt Cerberus in the Dry Valleys. Rocks from both localities have normal polarity magnetisations. These data, together with 15 other acceptable pole positions reported in the literature, define a Middle Jurassic paleomagnetic pole at 52°.7S, 139°.6W (u9s=4°A), which is not significantly different from previously reported mean Middle Jurassic paleomagnetic poles from East Antarctica. Paleomagnetic investigations in the Ohio Range of mafic inclusions in Ordovician granitic and sedimentary rocks of Devonian and Permian ages found that the rocks are magnetically unstable and are unreliable for determining a paleomagnetic pole. Ordovician granitic basement rocks (Treves 1965) compose most of the steep escarpment, and are overlain by a mostly flat lying, 1200 m thick sequence of nonmetamorphosed sedimentary rocks of Devonian and Permian age (Long 1965; Bradshaw et al. 1984; McCartan et al. 1986). Abstract Two well-defined virtual geomagnetic poles (VGPs) for East Antarctica were obtained from the Middle Jurassic Ferrar Dolerite, sampled from a thick sill on Mt Schopf in the Ohio Range, and from a horizontal sheet intruding Paleozoic granitic rocks at Mt Cerberus in the Dry Valleys. The VGP from the sill at Mt Schopf lies at lat. 58°.0S, long. 129°.0W (dm=13°, dp=12°), and the VGP from Mt Cerberus lies at lat. 57°.8S, long. 135°.7W (dm=6°, dp=6°). Rocks from both localities have normal polarity magnetisations. These data, together with 15 other acceptable pole positions reported in the literature, define a Middle Jurassic paleomagnetic pole at 52°.7S, 139°.6W (u9s=4°A), which is not significantly different from previously reported mean Middle Jurassic paleomagnetic poles from East Antarctica. Paleomagnetic investigations in the Ohio Range of mafic inclusions in Ordovician granitic and sedimentary rocks of Devonian and Permian ages found that the rocks are magnetically unstable and are unreliable for determining a paleomagnetic pole. GEOLOGIC SETTING Ohio Range The Ohio Range comprises a prominent 1000 m granitic escarpment separating the Polar Plateau to the south from the great ice sheet of Marie Byrd Land to the north (Fig. 1).
